title: In praise of boredom?
subtitle: Psychologists are reconsidering an emotion that most of us go to great lengths to avoid

paragraphs.text: Few states of mind have been so consistently maligned as boredom. Kierkegaard, writing in the 1840s, had one of his characters describe it as the root of all evil, and Schopenhauer regarded it as evidence that human existence has no intrinsic worth. Modern societies, for their part, have invested enormous ingenuity in its abolition. A smartphone, whatever else it may be, is a device which ensures that nobody need ever again spend a minute with nothing to attend to. It is a curious paradox, then, that just as we have acquired the means to banish boredom almost entirely, a number of psychologists have begun to argue that it may be worth preserving.

Part of the difficulty in assessing such claims is that, until relatively recently, boredom attracted remarkably little scientific attention. It was regarded as too trivial, too fleeting and too subjective to merit serious study, and even those researchers who did take an interest could not agree on what it was. Some treated it as a property of situations – a monotonous task, a long wait – while others saw it as a trait of personality, measurable by questionnaires designed to identify individuals who are easily bored. Only in the last two decades has a broad consensus emerged that boredom is best understood as the experience of wanting to engage with something satisfying while being unable to do so.

That the experience is genuinely unpleasant is not in doubt. In a widely reported series of experiments conducted at the University of Virginia, participants were asked to sit alone in a bare room with nothing to do but think for between six and fifteen minutes. When given the option of administering a mild electric shock to themselves during that period, a substantial proportion – around two-thirds of the men and a quarter of the women – chose to do so, even though they had earlier said they would pay money to avoid such a shock. It is hard to imagine a more vivid demonstration of how strongly people prefer almost any stimulation to none.

Chronic proneness to boredom, moreover, keeps uncomfortable company. People who report being bored frequently are, on average, more likely to suffer from depression and anxiety, to gamble compulsively, to overeat and to misuse alcohol and drugs. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that boredom causes these problems. The associations are correlational, and it is equally plausible that some underlying difficulty – in regulating attention, perhaps, or in identifying what one actually wants – gives rise both to frequent boredom and to the behaviours that accompany it.

It is against this rather bleak background that the case for boredom's usefulness has been made, and it takes two quite distinct forms. The first, and by far the more popular, holds that boredom fosters creativity. In one frequently cited study, volunteers who had spent a quarter of an hour copying numbers out of a telephone directory subsequently generated more ideas in a test of imaginative thinking than those who had not. Taken up enthusiastically by journalists and self-help authors, the notion that a bored mind is a fertile one has acquired the status of folk wisdom.

The evidence, it must be said, is thinner than this enthusiasm suggests. The original experiments involved modest numbers of participants, the measures of creativity they employed were narrow, and attempts to reproduce the results have yielded mixed outcomes. Even if the effect is real, it may owe less to boredom itself than to the mind-wandering that tends to accompany it, and mind-wandering can be cultivated in far more agreeable ways – on a walk, say, or in the shower.

The second argument strikes me as considerably more persuasive. It holds that boredom functions much as pain or hunger do: as a signal. Physical pain is disagreeable precisely so that we will withdraw a hand from the flame; boredom, on this account, is disagreeable so that we will abandon an activity that has ceased to serve our goals and look for one that does. Dr Lucia Ferrante, a psychologist who has studied the emotion for many years, describes it as ‘a kind of internal alarm that tells us our attention is being wasted’. Seen in this light, boredom is not a failing of character but a valuable piece of information, and a person who never experienced it would not have overcome a weakness so much as lost a sense.

If this is right, it has implications for how we ought to respond to boredom. A signal is useful only if it is heeded, and the trouble with the limitless supply of distraction offered by our devices is not that it prevents boredom but that it silences the alarm without addressing its cause. Reaching for a phone in every idle moment resembles taking painkillers for a broken leg: the discomfort recedes, but nothing is mended.

None of this amounts to a celebration of tedium. Boredom imposed by circumstances one is powerless to change – the prisoner's cell, the soul-destroying job – offers no such opportunity, and in those settings it is closer to suffering than to information. Nor should parents conclude that leaving children with nothing to do is a reliable route to creativity. The lesson is more modest: that boredom, like other uncomfortable emotions, deserves to be listened to before it is dismissed. We have become remarkably adept at making it go away. We might do better to ask what it is trying to tell us.

items.stem: In the first paragraph, the writer suggests that modern technology
options: has made people more likely to feel bored.
was developed mainly as a form of entertainment.
allows people to avoid boredom almost completely.
has changed the way philosophers regard boredom.
items.evidence: just as we have acquired the means to banish boredom almost entirely
items.note: A reverses the writer's point; D borrows the philosophers from earlier in the paragraph but the text links them to no change caused by technology.

items.stem: According to the second paragraph, why did scientists pay little attention to boredom in the past?
options: It was considered too unimportant to be worth investigating.
It could only be measured by means of questionnaires.
It was seen as a sign of an unhealthy personality.
It was thought to be caused only by dull situations.
items.evidence: It was regarded as too trivial, too fleeting and too subjective to merit serious study
items.note: B and D distort details: questionnaires and monotonous situations are mentioned only as ways some researchers defined boredom.

items.stem: What is the writer's purpose in describing the experiments at the University of Virginia?
options: to show that people misjudge how they will react to pain
to illustrate how much people dislike having nothing to occupy them
to question the methods used in research into boredom
to compare the ways in which men and women cope with boredom
items.evidence: It is hard to imagine a more vivid demonstration of how strongly people prefer almost any stimulation to none.
items.note: The figures for men and women (D) are given as detail; the writer draws no comparison between the sexes.

items.stem: What point does the writer make about people who are often bored?
options: They tend to underestimate how frequently they feel bored.
Their boredom is the main reason for their other difficulties.
They are less likely than others to seek help for depression.
Their boredom and their other problems may have a shared origin.
items.evidence: it is equally plausible that some underlying difficulty – in regulating attention, perhaps, or in identifying what one actually wants – gives rise both to frequent boredom and to the behaviours that accompany it
items.note: B is the conclusion the writer explicitly warns against: 'It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that boredom causes these problems.'

items.statement: The belief that boredom stimulates creative thinking has become widely accepted.
items.evidence: the notion that a bored mind is a fertile one has acquired the status of folk wisdom

items.statement: The research linking boredom to creativity was based on large samples.
items.evidence: The original experiments involved modest numbers of participants

items.statement: People's minds are more likely to wander when they are outdoors than when they are indoors.
items.note: A walk and a shower are offered only as pleasant ways of encouraging mind-wandering; the writer makes no comparison between outdoor and indoor settings.

items.statement: The view of boredom as a warning signal is more convincing than the view that it promotes creativity.
items.evidence: The second argument strikes me as considerably more persuasive.

items.statement: Turning to a phone whenever boredom arises deals with the reason for the feeling.
items.evidence: it silences the alarm without addressing its cause
items.note: The writer says distraction removes the discomfort but leaves the cause untouched, like painkillers for a broken leg.

items.statement: Children who are frequently bored tend to do less well at school.
items.note: Children are mentioned only in relation to creativity; nothing is said about their performance at school.
